obsequious

ob-SEE-kwee-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Obsequious is excessively eager to please or obey someone, often through flattery.

The obsequious salesman agreed with every complaint the customer made, hoping to close the sale.

Example

The obsequious courtier bowed lower and laughed harder at the king's jokes than anyone else in the room.

Obsequious describes flattery so excessive it becomes uncomfortable or insincere to witness.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fawning: Fawning is the flattery itself — the gushing compliments, the too-eager agreement. Obsequious describes the whole manner behind it: an obsequious person doesn't just flatter but rushes to please and agree in every possible way. Fawning names the behavior; obsequious names the character it reveals.

servile: Servile means acting like a servant — obeying instantly and placing yourself beneath someone, even with no flattery at all. Obsequious adds the eager flattery: the compliments, the laughter, the endless agreement meant to win favor. A servile clerk just submits; an obsequious one flatters while submitting.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dignified: having a calm, serious manner worthy of respect

assertive: confidently expressing oneself without excessive deference

Where it sits · how far the flattery goes — polite → obsequious → sycophantic

polite vs. obsequious: Polite is basic everyday courtesy; obsequious pushes far past that into excessive, uncomfortable flattery.

sycophantic vs. obsequious: Sycophantic goes even further than obsequious, implying flattery aimed purely at selfish personal gain.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ob-

prefix — ob-: toward (Latin)

root — sequ

root — sequ: to follow (Latin (sequi))

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: ob- ('toward') + sequ ('to follow') + -ious together mean 'following toward' someone eagerly -- the fawning behavior obsequious describes.

Use the root in a new word: sequel

Use the root in a new word: sequel: Sequel shares the same Latin root sequi ('to follow'), describing a story that follows after the original.

Word Choice

Obsequious is almost always critical -- it describes fawning behavior meant to win favor, not genuine kindness. Its synonym servile was taught in Unit 58: servile emphasizes slave-like compliance, while obsequious emphasizes eager flattery.
